message:
SITUATION:
Our engineering department went fully remote at the start of the year. In the following quarter, tickets closed per engineer fell 10% compared with the quarter before. Our VP says this proves remote work lowered productivity and wants people back in the office. In the same quarter, though, we hired four new engineers who were still onboarding, and the team switched to writing bigger tickets that bundle several tasks. I think the VP is wrong, and it's obviously just the new hires dragging the average down. Can you settle this for us?

CLAIM:
Going remote lowered the engineering team's productivity.

RESPONSE:
# I can't settle it from this, and neither can your VP

You and your VP are both claiming more than the data shows. In one quarter, three things changed at once:

1. **Remote work** (the VP's explanation)
2. **Four onboarding hires** (your explanation)
3. **Bigger tickets that bundle several tasks**

All three predict fewer tickets closed per engineer. With one before/after comparison, you can't tell them apart.

## Why each side's claim is too strong

**The VP:** A 10% drop that coincides with going remote doesn't prove remote work caused it, especially when two other changes would produce the same drop.

**You:** New hires may not be the main cause. The ticket change is arguably the strongest candidate, because it changes the measuring stick itself. If the average ticket now holds 1.5 old tasks, closing 10% fewer tickets means about 35% *more* work got done. Whether the new hires could explain 10% depends on team size, which you haven't told me:

| Engineers before | After (+4, near-zero output) | Drop from new hires alone |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | 24 | ~17% (more than the whole drop) |
| 36 | 40 | ~10% (all of it) |
| 60 | 64 | ~6% (part of it) |

That table assumes new hires closed nothing and everyone else held steady. Onboarding also costs senior engineers time, so the real effect may be larger.

## What would settle it

In rough order of value:

1. **Hold the team constant.** Compare tickets per engineer for only the engineers who were there in both quarters. This removes the new-hire effect entirely.
2. **Hold the unit constant.** Measure work in something that didn't change: tasks or subtasks completed, story points (if estimation stayed consistent), merged PRs, or deploys. Or estimate how many old-style tasks the average new ticket contains.
3. **Look at more than two quarters.** A single quarter-over-quarter change could just be seasonal (holidays, planning cycles, a big release). Check last year's same transition and the trend before remote.
4. **Use other output signals.** Cycle time, deployment frequency, and incident rates are harder to distort with ticket bookkeeping.
5. **Find a comparison group, if one exists.** Another team that went remote without hiring or changing tickets, or one that stayed in-office, would be the closest thing to a controlled test.

If tenured engineers' output, measured in consistent units, held steady or rose, the remote-work claim loses its support. If it fell noticeably, the VP has a real point, though seasonality would still need ruling out.

If you can share the raw numbers (per-engineer ticket counts with start dates, plus some measure of ticket size), I can run these breakdowns for you.
